notes.definition: Alcohols are a homologous series of compounds containing the functional group –OH. The first four are methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol. Aqueous ethanol is made by fermenting sugar solutions with yeast.
explanation: Alcohols are organic compounds that contain the –OH functional group. The first four members of the homologous series are methanol (CH₃OH), ethanol (C₂H₅OH, also written CH₃CH₂OH), propanol (C₃H₇OH) and butanol (C₄H₉OH). Their general formula can be written CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH. Alcohols are not hydrocarbons because they contain oxygen. They can be represented by formulae such as CH₃CH₂OH, or by displayed formulae that show the O–H bond.

Because they share the same functional group, alcohols have similar chemical reactions. With sodium, an alcohol reacts to give off hydrogen gas, so you see fizzing (effervescence) and the sodium slowly disappears. The reaction is less vigorous than sodium with water. Alcohols burn in air: complete combustion produces carbon dioxide and water and releases energy, for example C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O, so alcohols are used as fuels. They burn with a clean, almost colourless or pale blue flame.

Methanol, ethanol and propanol dissolve in water to form a neutral solution with a pH of 7; butanol is less soluble. When an alcohol reacts with an oxidising agent, such as acidified potassium dichromate, it is oxidised to a carboxylic acid. For example, ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid. This also happens slowly when wine is left open to the air, because microbes oxidise the ethanol, turning the wine sour like vinegar.

Aqueous solutions of ethanol are produced by fermentation. Yeast is added to a sugar solution (such as glucose) and kept warm, at about 30 °C (between about 25 °C and 35 °C), with air kept out (anaerobic conditions) and a slightly acidic pH. Enzymes in the yeast convert the glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. If it is too cold, the reaction is slow; if it is too hot, the enzymes are denatured. Oxygen must be excluded, otherwise the ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid.

Alcohols have many uses. Methanol and ethanol are used as fuels; ethanol can be mixed with petrol for cars. Alcohols are good solvents, for example in perfumes, inks and medicines, because they dissolve many substances that water cannot. Ethanol is the main alcohol in alcoholic drinks such as beer and wine. Methanol is also an important feedstock for making other chemicals, but it is very toxic to drink.
keyFacts: First four alcohols: methanol CH₃OH, ethanol C₂H₅OH, propanol C₃H₇OH, butanol C₄H₉OH.
Alcohol + sodium: fizzing, hydrogen gas produced.
Alcohols burn in air to give CO₂ and H₂O: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.
Methanol, ethanol and propanol dissolve in water to form neutral solutions (pH 7).
Alcohol + oxidising agent → carboxylic acid (ethanol → ethanoic acid).
Fermentation: yeast, sugar solution, about 30 °C, no oxygen: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂.
Uses: fuels, solvents; ethanol is the main alcohol in alcoholic drinks.

keyTerms.definition: An organic compound containing the –OH functional group, such as ethanol.
The group of atoms that gives a homologous series its characteristic reactions; –OH for alcohols.
The conversion of sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide by enzymes in yeast, without oxygen.
A substance that oxidises another substance; it turns alcohols into carboxylic acids.
A liquid that dissolves other substances; alcohols are widely used as solvents.
When the shape of an enzyme's active site is changed (for example by high temperature) so that it no longer works.

workedExamples.title: Balancing alcohol combustion
workedExamples.question: Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of butanol, C₄H₉OH.
steps: Oxygen needed on the right: 8 + 5 = 13 O atoms. The alcohol already supplies 1 O, so O₂ must supply 12 O atoms = 6O₂.

workedExamples.title: Predicting reactions of propanol
workedExamples.question: Predict what you would see when a small piece of sodium is added to propanol, and name the gas.
steps: All alcohols have the –OH group, so they react in the same way as ethanol.
The sodium fizzes slowly and gets smaller.
The gas is hydrogen (it gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint).
workedExamples.answer: Fizzing (bubbles) as hydrogen is given off; the sodium slowly disappears.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think alcohols are alkaline because they contain 'OH'.
misconceptions.right: In fact the –OH in an alcohol is covalently bonded, not a hydroxide ion, so alcohol solutions are neutral (pH 7).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think alcohols are hydrocarbons.
misconceptions.right: In fact alcohols contain oxygen as well as carbon and hydrogen, so they are not hydrocarbons.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think fermentation works faster the hotter it is.
misconceptions.right: In fact above about 35 °C to 40 °C the yeast enzymes start to denature, so fermentation slows and stops.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think oxygen is needed for fermentation.
misconceptions.right: In fact fermentation is anaerobic; with oxygen the ethanol would be oxidised to ethanoic acid.

realWorld: Bioethanol made by fermenting sugar cane is blended with petrol as a fuel (E10 petrol contains up to 10% ethanol).
Ethanol is used as a solvent in perfumes, hand sanitisers and medicines.
Wine turns to vinegar when ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid by microbes in the air.
separateOnlyContent: All of this subtopic is for separate Chemistry (8462) only; Combined Science does not cover alcohols.
examTips: Learn the fermentation conditions as a set: yeast, sugar solution, warm (about 30 °C), anaerobic.
For the reaction with sodium, give the observation (fizzing) and the gas (hydrogen).
When balancing alcohol combustion, remember the alcohol already contains one oxygen atom.
Alcohol + oxidising agent gives a carboxylic acid with the same number of carbon atoms: ethanol → ethanoic acid.
summary: First four: methanol, ethanol, propanol, butanol.
With sodium they fizz, giving hydrogen.
They burn to give CO₂ and water, so are used as fuels.
They dissolve in water to give neutral solutions.
Ethanol is made by fermenting sugar with yeast at about 30 °C without oxygen.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the displayed formula of ethanol.
What is the functional group of the alcohols?
questions.explanation: Alcohols contain –OH. –COOH is the carboxylic acid group and –COO– is the ester link.

questions.question: What is the formula of ethanol?
questions.explanation: Ethanol has two carbon atoms and an –OH group. CH₃OH is methanol, C₂H₆ is ethane and CH₃COOH is ethanoic acid.

questions.question:
Sodium reacts with ethanol.
Which gas is produced?
questions.explanation: Sodium reacts with the –OH group, releasing hydrogen gas, so the mixture fizzes.

questions.question:
Ethanol can be made by fermenting sugar solution.
What is added to the sugar solution to ferment it?
questions.explanation: Enzymes in yeast convert sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide. Steam with a catalyst makes ethanol from ethene instead.

questions.question:
Ethanol is dissolved in water.
What is the pH of the solution?
questions.explanation: Alcohols dissolve to give neutral solutions. The –OH group is not a hydroxide ion, so the solution is not alkaline.

questions.question: Which temperature is most suitable for fermentation?
questions.explanation: Yeast enzymes work best when warm. At 5 °C the reaction is very slow; at 70 °C and above the enzymes are denatured.

questions.question:
Ethanol reacts with an oxidising agent.
What is formed?
questions.explanation: Oxidation of an alcohol gives a carboxylic acid with the same number of carbon atoms.

questions.question: Which equation is correctly balanced for the complete combustion of methanol?
questions.explanation: Per methanol: 1CO₂ and 2H₂O need 4 O atoms; methanol supplies 1, so 1½O₂. Doubling gives 2CH₃OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 4H₂O.

questions.explanation: With air present, ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid (and yeast respires aerobically). Heat, not oxygen, denatures enzymes.

questions.question:
Ethanol has the formula C₂H₅OH.
Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of ethanol.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): C = 12   H = 1   O = 16
questions.explanation: Count all six hydrogen atoms: five in C₂H₅ and one in OH. 24 + 6 + 16 = 46.

questions.question:
Ethanol burns completely in oxygen.
C₂H₅OH + xO₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O
What is the value of x in the balanced equation?
questions.explanation: O atoms on the right: 4 + 3 = 7. Ethanol supplies 1, so O₂ supplies 6 atoms: 3O₂.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the displayed formula of propanol, C₃H₇OH.
Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of propanol.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): C = 12   H = 1   O = 16
questions.explanation: 36 + 8 + 16 = 60. Propanol has 8 hydrogen atoms in total.

questions.question:
Butanol burns completely in oxygen.
C₄H₉OH + yO₂ → 4CO₂ + 5H₂O
Calculate the value of y in the balanced equation.
markScheme: 1 mark: O atoms on the right = 8 + 5 = 13
questions.explanation: Remember the oxygen atom already in butanol. 12 ÷ 2 = 6.

questions.question:
Glucose is fermented to produce ethanol.
C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂
Calculate the mass of ethanol produced when 180 g of glucose is fully fermented.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): C = 12   H = 1   O = 16
markScheme: 1 mark: Mr glucose = 180, so 1 mol glucose
questions.explanation: 1 mol of glucose gives 2 mol of ethanol (Mr 46). The other 88 g is carbon dioxide (2 × 44), so mass is conserved.

questions.question: Give two uses of alcohols.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: fuels; solvents; (ethanol in) alcoholic drinks; feedstock for other chemicals
questions.explanation: Alcohols burn well (fuels), dissolve many substances (solvents), and ethanol is the alcohol in drinks.

questions.question: Give three conditions needed to make ethanol by fermentation.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any three: yeast; sugar (glucose) solution; warm, about 25 to 35 °C; absence of oxygen (anaerobic); slightly acidic pH
questions.explanation: Yeast enzymes need warmth and the absence of oxygen to produce ethanol.

questions.question:
A small piece of sodium is added to propanol.
Describe what you would see.
questions.explanation: Alcohols react with sodium like water but less vigorously, releasing hydrogen.

questions.question:
Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, is fermented to produce ethanol and carbon dioxide.
Write the balanced symbol equation for this reaction.
questions.explanation: Check: 6 C, 12 H and 6 O on each side.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the formulae of three alcohols.
Explain why these alcohols are described as a homologous series.
markScheme: 1 mark: same functional group (–OH) / same general formula
1 mark: similar chemical reactions / each differs by CH₂
questions.explanation: The –OH group gives them similar reactions, and each member has one more CH₂ than the last.

questions.explanation: Fermentation depends on yeast enzymes, which are denatured at high temperatures.

questions.question:
Ethanol for fuel can be made by fermentation of sugar or by the hydration of ethene.
Suggest one advantage of making ethanol by fermentation.
markScheme: 1 mark: uses a renewable raw material (sugar from plants) / does not use crude oil
1 mark: low temperature and pressure so less energy needed
questions.explanation: Ethene comes from crude oil (finite), whereas sugar can be regrown. Fermentation runs at about 30 °C.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows apparatus used to make ethanol by fermentation.
Describe how ethanol is produced by fermentation.

markScheme: Indicative content: sugar (glucose) solution; yeast added; warm, about 30 °C (25 to 35 °C); anaerobic (no air), e.g. airlock; slightly acidic; enzymes in yeast catalyse the reaction; products ethanol and carbon dioxide; C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂; aqueous ethanol solution produced.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): reactants, at least two conditions and both products, possibly with the equation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as 'sugar and yeast make alcohol'.
questions.explanation: A top answer gives sugar and yeast, warm anaerobic conditions, and both products with the equation.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows four alcohols.
Describe what happens when an alcohol:
• reacts with sodium
• burns in air
• is added to water
• reacts with an oxidising agent.
Include equations for ethanol where you can.
markScheme: Indicative content: sodium: fizzing, hydrogen gas produced, sodium disappears, less vigorous than with water (2Na + 2C₂H₅OH → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂ for credit); burning: alcohols burn in air releasing energy, used as fuels, complete combustion gives CO₂ and H₂O, C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O; water: methanol, ethanol and propanol dissolve (mix completely), solution is neutral, pH 7, butanol less soluble; oxidising agent: e.g. acidified potassium dichromate, alcohol oxidised to carboxylic acid, ethanol → ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH); all show similar reactions because they share the –OH functional group.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all four reactions described accurately with observations or products, at least one balanced equation, and the link to the –OH functional group.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): three or four reactions described with some products, possibly with an error.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two reactions described simply.
questions.explanation: Cover all four reactions, give observations as well as products, and explain the similarity using the –OH group.

questions.question: Which feature is found in the displayed formula of every alcohol?
options: An O–H bond attached to a carbon atom
markScheme: 1 mark: O–H bond attached to a carbon atom
questions.explanation: Every alcohol contains a C–O–H group. A C=O bond appears in carboxylic acids.

questions.question:
Ethanol is oxidised.
Name the carboxylic acid formed.
questions.explanation: Oxidising ethanol forms ethanoic acid, the acid in vinegar.

questions.question: Which alcohol has four carbon atoms?
questions.explanation: But = 4 carbon atoms. Butanol is C₄H₉OH.
